newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czechs launch U.S.-retooled jet fighter.
newsitem.headline: Czechs launch U.S.-retooled jet fighter.

text.p: Czech aircraft maker Aero Vodochody on Thursday launched its western-upgraded L-159 light fighter jet and underlined the company's hopes of recovering from its deep financial problems.

The "L-ka", billed as a "multi-role combat aircraft", was unveiled at a hangar north of Prague as Defence Minister Miloslav Vyborny announced the government had agreed a long-expected, multi-billion crown order for 72 jets.
"This aicraft will be the backbone of the Czech airforce at the start of the 21st century," Vyborny said at the ceremony.
"It fulfils demands for a multi-purpose, sub-sonic jet... fully compatible with air forces of the (NATO) alliance."

Cash-strapped Aero has upgraded its Czech-made L39 and L59 aircraft that were based on Soviet-era designs with U. S. technology. Boeing Co unit Rockwell International provided avionics, engines came from Allied Signal Aerospace and components from other western suppliers.

The plane, which has yet to win any foreign orders, is geared towards NATO members and other potential clients looking for a NATO-compatible light aircraft with reconnaissance, anti-ship, close-air support and weapons capability.
The Czechs are upgrading their Cold War-era air fleet while preparing for membership in the North Atlantic Treaty Alliance.
The Czech Republic, Poland, and Hungary, are widely seen as likely candidates to be accepted for NATO membership at a July summit of the alliance in Madrid.

Czech hopes for purchasing more-expensive western built aircraft have become bogged down by debate over domestic budget cuts and rebuilding Aero as a company. The country is still considering buying more advanced jets, however.

The 72 planes are to be delivered to the Czech Army between 1999-2002, starting with five in 1999, 16 in 2000, 26 in 2001 and 25 in 2002, at a total price of around 23 billion crowns ($715.8 million) Aero chairman Jaroslav Borak told reporters.
Chief executive Adam Stranak said Aero needed to sell 150 planes to see a return on development costs.
"In the next five years there will be about 10 to 15 countries as potential customers... Our first foreign customer will probably be in Europe," Stranak added.

In May, the cabinet agreed to begin exclusive talks on selling a 34-40 percent stake in Aero Vodochody to a consortium of Boeing, McDonnell Douglas Corp. and the national airline Ceske Aerolinie a.s. (CSA).
Borak said Aero hoped to have the new shareholder structure in place by October, finalising talks with the Boeing-led consortium in September.

Under the plan under discussion, the Boeing consortium would hold 34 percent of Aero's basic equity worth 950 million crowns, with the Czech National Property Fund holding a similar stake, and the state-run Konsolidacni Banka the remaining 780 million crown in equity capital.
The government last year approved a 3.26 billion crown package clearing the heavily indebted company's books through Konsolidacni Banka in a debt for equity swap.
